newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Dissidents back U.S. statements on Iraq rift.
newsitem.headline: Dissidents back U.S. statements on Iraq rift.

text.p: Iraqi dissidents said on Thursday that recent U.S. statements on Iraq gave an accurate account of rifts in President Saddam Hussein's inner circle.

They said Washington's tough talk was meant to send a clear message from newly installed Clinton administration officials to Western allies and people inside Iraq that Saddam must go before any thaw in relations with Baghdad.

"The new U.S. administration is sending a clear message that there are no chances of normalisation with Baghdad as long as Saddam is in power," Hamid al-Bayati, spokesman of the Supreme Council for the Islamic Revolution in Iraq (SCIRI), told Reuters from London by telephone.
"It is also a signal to the ruling elite and army officers that Saddam has no future and that his status is not stable," he said.
Senior U.S. officials this week referred to Saddam as a "demon" and said there were signs of a power struggle in Baghdad.

"There are a great deal of complicated internal struggles for power" going on, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said in response to questions about an earlier statement by a senior U.S. military official.
The official had said that Saddam had put his wife under house arrest and was changing locations more often out of apparent fear for his safety.
An Iraqi government spokesman ridiculed the U.S. statements and said they were a "distortion and propaganda ploy against Iraq".

"The situation inside Iraq is very dangerous," another Iraqi opposition figure, Saad al-Jaber, said by telephone from London. "Things could get out of Saddam's hands soon and the indications are all there."
Jaber, leader of a group called the Free Iraq Council, said an assassination attempt that badly wounded Saddam's eldest son Uday on December 12 was a significant development.
"We know that no coup against Saddam can succeed with Uday around, so those who carried out the professional operation had greater plans.
"I tell you at least 90 percent of the officers inside the army want to get rid of him (Saddam). His family is also in turmoil," Jaber said.

Bayati said the internal rift had deepened since Saddam ordered the killing of his two sons-in-law, Hussein Kamel Hassan and Saddam Kamel Hassan, when they returned to Baghdad in February 1996, months after they defected to Jordan.
Iraq said at the time that the two were killed by relatives angered by their defection.
"Many people in the family and around Saddam did not approve the killings because the two men were given guarantees that they would not be harmed if they returned to Baghdad," he said.

"That's when many in Saddam's inner circle -- even his first wife and daughters -- realised that he must go. Saddam later tried to satisfy them by declaring the two slain men 'martyrs of anger' and paid blood money to their families."

Bayati said Saddam had recently tried to portray himself to his people as an internationally accepted leader, especially after a deal with the United Nations that allowed Iraq to sell oil worth $2 billion every six months in return for food and medicine.
The deal, signed last May, went into effect in December.
Baghdad has been under stringent U.N. sanctions since it invaded Kuwait in 1990.
"The U.S. statements mean that there is no hope that Saddam will be accepted in the West and that the Iraqi people and army must act," Bayati said.
